knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: CT-R1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Let X1, ..., Xn be iid with finite mean mu and finite positive variance sigma squared. What does the central limit theorem state?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: The CLT concerns the centred and scaled sample mean or sum.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: The standardised sample mean converges in distribution to N(0,1).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Applying the limit to observations or omitting standardisation.

choices.label: sqrt(n)(sample mean minus mu)/sigma converges in distribution to a standard Normal variable as n grows.
The sample mean equals mu with probability 1 for every finite n.
Each Xi becomes Normally distributed as n grows.
The unstandardised sum converges to standard Normal without centring or scaling.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: CT-R1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. The underlying observations are highly skewed but have finite variance. Which statement about their sample mean is justified?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Finite-variance skewed data can satisfy the CLT, although strong skewness may require a larger sample.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Use the Normal approximation cautiously for sufficiently large n.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Assuming every sample mean is exactly Normal.

choices.label: For sufficiently large n, the standardised mean may be approximated by standard Normal, but the approximation is not generally exact at finite n.
The sample mean is exactly Normal for every n because a mean was calculated.
The CLT cannot apply to any skewed distribution.
Increasing n makes the original observations less skewed.
